query: For high-entropy alloys intended for harsh corrosive mechanical environments, what single mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs resistance to simultaneous wear and corrosion, and why? Propose a controlled comparison that would test the hypothesis, predict how combined degradation and its wear and corrosion components would differ from a matched baseline, define where the prediction should hold or fail, identify supporting prior evidence, and state an observation that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In high‐entropy alloys for harsh, corrosive mechanical environments, wear continuously exposes fresh surfaces that rapidly form a passivating oxide film enriched in corrosion‐resistant elements (e.g., Cr, Mo). This adaptive tribo-corrosion passivation mechanism reduces both abrasion and corrosive degradation by continuously regenerating a protective layer that mitigates further attack.
generation.material_initial_state: A nanocrystalline, dual-phase (or homogeneously solid‐solution) refractory or corrosion‐resistant HEA containing elements known to form stable oxides (such as Cr and Mo) uniformly distributed.
generation.intervention: Subject samples to simultaneous mechanical wear (e.g., sliding or abrasive contact) and a corrosive environment (such as an acidic solution or molten salt) under controlled temperature conditions.
generation.conditions: Testing under conditions that mimic harsh operational environments (elevated temperature, moderate wear rate, and chemically aggressive media) where the passive film can be disrupted and reformed repeatedly.
generation.structural_mediator: The dynamically reformed passivating oxide film, which arises from the segregation of specific, corrosion‐resistant elements at wear-exposed surfaces and grain boundaries.
generation.mechanism: During wear, the mechanical removal of the native oxide triggers segregation of elements that preferentially oxidize to form a new, robust surface film. This quickly reestablished layer not only protects against chemical corrosion but also offers mechanical resistance against further material removal.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to a matched HEA baseline that does not have efficient element segregation and passivation, the alloy with this mechanism should exhibit a lower net material loss when subjected to combined wear and corrosion; the degradation rate under simultaneous exposure will be less than the sum of the individual wear and corrosion rates.
generation.baseline: A high-entropy alloy of similar composition but lacking the element partitioning or segregation propensity (and hence rapid passivation) which results in higher cumulative degradation under identical test conditions.
generation.boundary: This protective mechanism should be effective when the wear rate is moderate enough to allow timely reformation of the passivating film. In conditions of extreme mechanical abrasion or highly aggressive chemistry that outpaces film formation, the advantage could diminish or fail.
generation.uncertainty: The precise kinetics of the segregation-driven film reformation, the influence of specific alloying elements, and the interplay between film durability and reformation rate under varying operational regimes require further quantification.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two HEA variants: one engineered to promote corrosion-resistant element segregation (and hence passivation) and a control alloy with similar bulk composition but reduced segregation/passivation tendencies. Expose both to identical tests involving simultaneous mechanical wear (e.g., reciprocating sliding) and immersion in a corrosive medium at an elevated temperature. Periodically measure material loss, and characterize the surface films using spectroscopic methods.
measurements: Corrosion rate (electrochemical measurements such as potentiodynamic polarization)
Surface film composition and thickness (using XPS, TEM, or SEM/EDS)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the alloy designed for rapid passivation does not show a significantly lower combined wear-corrosion degradation rate compared to the control, or if surface analyses do not reveal the formation of a robust, passivating film correlated with improved performance, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: In this study, bulk samples of a CrMoNbWV high-entropy alloy (HEA) were obtained for the first time by spark plasma sintering (SPS) of mechanically alloyed (MA) powders at 1200 °C, 1300 °C, and 1400 °C. Microstructure evolution, phase formation as well as wear and corrosion behavior were investigated. The MA powders’ phase composition was found to be represented by body-centered-cubic (BCC) solid solution. The solid solution partially decomposed to Laves phases under the sintering, such as Cr 2 Nb and (Fe, Cr)Nb, and NbVO 4 -VO oxides mixture. The temperature increase to 1400 °C led to a grain coarsening of the BCC phase and decreased the Laves phase content accompanied by precipitation at the grain boundaries. The sintered samples showed high hardness and compressive strength (2700–2800 MPa) at room temperature. The wear tests demonstrated excellent results in comparison to conventional wear-resistant composites. The obtained samples also exhibited high corrosion resistance under electrochemical tests in H 2 SO 4 solution. The CrMoNbWV HEA has comparable mechanical and corrosive properties with the WNbMoTaV type HEA, but at the same time has a reduced density: CrMoNbWV—10.55 g/cm

Abstract The growing interest in refractory high-entropy alloys (HEAs) in the last decade is mainly due to their thermal stability, outstanding mechanical properties, and excellent corrosion resistance. However, currently HEAs are still not considered for use as common structural materials due to their inherent drawbacks in terms of processing and machining operations. The recent progress witnessed in additive manufacturing (AM) technologies has raised the option of producing complex components made of HEAs with minimal machining processes. So far, this could be achieved by using pre-alloyed powders of HEAs that were mainly produced by a conventional arc melting furnace (AMF) in the form of small compounds that were transformed into powder via a gas atomization process. To significantly reduce the production cost, the present study aims to analyze the ability to synthesize HEA WTaMoNbV via a laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) process using mixed elemental alloying powder as the raw material. Abstract Dual-phase high entropy alloys have recently attracted widespread attention as advanced structural materials due to their unique microstructure, excellent mechanical properties, and corrosion resistance. However, their molten salt corrosion behavior has not been reported, which is critical in evaluating their application merit in the areas of concentrating solar power and nuclear energy. Here, the molten salt corrosion behavior of AlCoCrFeNi 2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA) was evaluated in molten NaCl-KCl-MgCl 2 salt at 450 °C and 650 °C in comparison to conventional duplex stainless steel 2205 (DS2205). The EHEA showed a significantly lower corrosion rate of ~1 mm/year at 450 °C compared to ~8 mm/year for DS2205. Similarly, EHEA showed a lower corrosion rate of ~9 mm/year at 650 °C compared to ~20 mm/year for DS2205. There was selective dissolution of the body-centered cubic phase in both the alloys, B2 in AlCoCrFeNi 2.1 and α-Ferrite in DS2205. This was attributed to micro-galvanic coupling between the two phases in each alloy that was measured in terms of Volta potential difference using a scanning kelvin probe.
